title: Write a program to solve a 9×9 Sudoku board by filling empty cells so that every row, column, and 3×3 box contains the digits 1–9 exactly once.
shortTitle: Sudoku Solver — row, column, and box constraint checking

s1_definition.profdef: Backtracking over empty cells: find the next empty cell, try digits 1–9, place a digit only if it is absent from its row, column, and 3×3 box, then recurse. If the recursion fails, undo and try the next digit; if no digit works, return false to trigger backtracking higher up. The board is solved when no empty cell remains.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a 9-by-9 reconciliation grid at National Bank of India where each row, column, and sub-block must contain each code exactly once. You fill the first blank with a candidate that does not already appear in its row, column, or block, move on, and if you get stuck you erase and try a different candidate.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill each empty cell with a digit valid in its row, column, and box; recurse; undo on dead ends until the grid is complete.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backtracking over empty cells: find the next empty cell, try digits 1–9, place a digit only if it is absent from its row, column, and 3×3 box, then recurse. If the recursion fails, undo and try the next digit; if no digit works, return false to trigger backtracking higher up. The board is solved when no empty cell remains.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a 9-by-9 reconciliation grid at National Bank of India where each row, column, and sub-block must contain each code exactly once. You fill the first blank with a candidate that does not already appear in its row, column, or block, move on, and if you get stuck you erase and try a different candidate.

**One line to remember:** Fill each empty cell with a digit valid in its row, column, and box; recurse; undo on dead ends until the grid is complete.

sections.s2_technical:
Scan for an empty cell (a dot). For each digit one to nine, check validity against the same row, column, and the 3×3 box whose top-left is `(r/3)*3, (c/3)*3`. If valid, place it and recurse; if the recursion returns true the board is solved, otherwise reset the cell to empty and try the next digit. For example: `if (isValid(board,r,c,d)) { board[r][c]=d; if (solve(board)) return true; board[r][c]='.'; }`.

Returning true all the way up on the first complete fill stops the search, since Sudoku asks for one solution. The box index arithmetic maps any cell to its 3×3 region for the uniqueness check.

The worst-case time is exponential, but real puzzles are solved quickly because the row/column/box checks prune most branches immediately. A senior nuance is the minimum-remaining-value heuristic (fill the most constrained cell first), which dramatically speeds up hard puzzles.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a 9-by-9 reconciliation grid must be completed so each row, column, and sub-block holds each code exactly once, and the tool must fill the blanks automatically. This is exactly how a Sudoku solver works.

Problem 2 — A candidate code is only valid if it does not already appear in its row, column, or block, and the solver must undo bad guesses. This is exactly why validity is checked three ways and cells are reset on failure.

The mini-project builds a `ReconGridSolver`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a standard partially filled 9-by-9 grid.

Step 1: The solver finds the first empty cell at row zero column two and tries digits one upward.

Step 2: It checks each candidate against the row, the column, and the containing 3-by-3 box, placing the first valid one and recursing.

Step 3: When a later cell has no valid digit, the recursion returns false and the offending earlier cell is reset to empty and advanced to its next candidate.

Step 4: Eventually every cell is filled consistently; with no empty cell left, the solver returns true and the grid is fully reconciled.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  find '.' → try d=1..9
    isValid(row,col,box)? place → recurse
      solved deeper? return TRUE  (propagate up)
      else reset '.' , next d
    no d fits → return FALSE (backtrack)
  no '.' left → TRUE (grid complete)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Sudoku solver is backtracking over the empty cells of the grid. I find the next empty cell, try the digits one through nine in it, and place a digit only when it does not already appear in that cell's row, its column, or its three-by-three box. After placing a valid digit I recurse; if the recursion eventually fills the whole grid I propagate true all the way up and stop, and if it gets stuck I reset the cell to empty and try the next digit. When a cell has no valid digit at all I return false, which triggers backtracking in the caller.

The box-index arithmetic, taking row over three times three and column over three times three, maps any cell to its region for the uniqueness check. Real puzzles solve quickly because the three-way validity check prunes most candidates immediately, even though the worst case is exponential.

In my project at National Bank of India, a nine-by-nine reconciliation grid had to be completed so each row, column, and sub-block contained each code exactly once, and the tool filled the blanks automatically. This constraint backtracking solved it reliably, and for the hardest grids I applied the minimum-remaining-value heuristic, always filling the most constrained cell first, which cut the search time sharply.
